segments.text: The fake city was real. The proof was in a letter that had been handled so many times
the fold lines had worn through on one side, and the paper opened there without being told.
Not all the way. Paper that old does not fall open dramatically. It releases.
Along the crease where a thumb had pressed and pressed again over years of returning.
The fibre had given way to something thinner than paper. Thinner than intention.
And the letter understood its own opening. The way a door understands when someone who has come
through it a thousand times is approaching. The fold found its position before the hand arrived.
The person holding it, this matters so stay with it, was not holding the letter the way you hold
something you are about to read. The body position was wrong for reading. The elbows were bent inward,
the forearms parallel, both hands cupped around the paper as if the paper were a living thing that
might startle and require steadying. This was the grip of someone who had been surprised once
and had not been able to afford surprise again. February 1894. That was the date visible in the
upper left corner, the month and year in faded ink. And below it a name, James Coburn. The ink had the
sepia quality of something written when what we call sepia was simply what ink looked like when
it aged. Not a stylistic choice, not a filter applied to simulate the past, but the past itself,
drying out. The water stain in the upper right corner was oval,
approximately the size of a thumb pressed sideways. The ink beneath it was blurred but intact.
The stain had arrived at an angle that missed the line of text, blurring only the margin,
leaving the words themselves readable. The person holding the letter had noticed this the
first time they read it. They had thought about what the oval stain meant, where the water had come
from, where the Coburn had been caught in weather while writing, or whether the stain had arrived
later during one of the many hands through which this document had travelled between 1894
and now. They had never resolved this. They had learned to look at the oval the way you learn
to look at a question that has no answer, steadily, without demanding a resolution.
What were the walls of the white city made of? That is where this investigation begins,
with a letter worn through at the fold lines and a question that sounds simple enough,
and a labourer named James Coburn who found the answer with his hands before he had language for
it. The letter did not start with a declaration. It started with a practical problem. He wrote,
I am writing regarding the work on the south wing section of the manufacturer's building,
and certain things I have found that I did not expect to find and that are causing me trouble
on account of the plaster not behaving the way the specifications say it should behave.
He wrote the way a careful working man writes when he is building a case,
not with flourish, not with drama, but with the patient accumulation of specific observation
that might someday serve as documentation in a dispute over billing. He had no interest in mystery.
He had an interest in accuracy. These two things are not always separable.
Then toward the middle of the second page, it gave back more than it should have,
like ringing a pan and hearing a bell. The person holding the letter read this passage
one more time, not allowed. The lips moved slightly, the way lips move when reading something that
requires verification, when the mind needs the body's confirmation that the words are what they
appear to be. Then the letter was folded carefully along the lines it already knew. What were the
walls of the white city made of? May 1st, 1893. Jackson Park, Chicago. The shore of Lake Michigan,
south of the river. The lake wind had come off the water since morning,
and what it carried was not winter. Winter had released its hold on the lakefront by then,
but the specific cold that Lake Michigan produces in early May, the cold of water that has not yet
absorbed the season's warmth, water that is still operating on the thermal logic of March,
even though the calendar has moved past it. The temperature was cool enough for a coat,
but not cold enough to justify one, which is the specific meteorological category
that makes people stand around in crowds looking mildly underprepared. There were 20,000 people
in the Court of Honor. The official estimates would say somewhat less than that for the opening
ceremony. The formal count didn't include the crowds held back at the perimeter, waiting for
entry, watching the officials process between the buildings in their frock coats and top hat.
But inside the Court of Honor, in the open space between the great white buildings,
between the lagoon and the Calanade facades, and the gilded dome of the administration building
at the center of it all, 20,000 people standing in the dusk waiting for something to happen.
The buildings, at that hour, were shapes. The light had gone out of the western sky
about 40 minutes before the ceremony was scheduled to begin. And the Court of Honor buildings,
the agriculture building, the manufacturers and liberal arts building, the machinery hall,
all of them presenting their neoclassical facades to the lagoon,
had resolved into silhouette, great white silhouette. The columns and cornices and
pediments were still visible as shapes even after the light was gone, because the calcium
sulfate surface of the staff plaster had a quality that caught whatever residual illumination
remained in the sky and held it slightly longer than ordinary surfaces would. The buildings didn't
go dark when the sky went dark. They faded. And in the fading, they seemed paradoxically larger.
This was the moment before. The smell in the crowd, wool coats and the chemical perfume
of new paint not yet cured, and from somewhere beyond the lagoon, the smell of construction lumber.
The white city had been built in approximately 30 months, and the lumber hadn't had time to
fully integrate with the damp Chicago air. And it still announced itself in gaps between the
decorative surfaces where rain had gotten in and encouraged the wood to release its own
character into the atmosphere. There was also food. The concession stands along the midway
pleasant's had been open since the afternoon, and the smell of fried things moved through the
crowd in gusts whenever the lake wind shifted. And the sound of the crowd, not silence. The
specific sound of 20,000 people simultaneously deciding not to speak. The baseline was still there.
Coughs, children, the creek of dress shoes against flagstone, the distant clatter of the midway.
But the conversational layer had been withdrawn, held in reserve for the moment that was about to
arrive. The buildings were dark. Then President Grover Cleveland pressed the gilded telegraph key.
What happened next was not gradual. That is the detail the photographs cannot convey,
the detail that the account in the official program hadn't adequately prepared the crowd for,
the detail that separated the memory of those who were present from the understanding of those
who arrived later through images. The Westinghouse Tesla alternating current system,
the complete polyphase system. The first time such a system had been deployed for general
illumination at this scale, didn't warm up. It didn't flicker on from dim to bright over the
course of seconds. When the circuit closed, the lamps came alive all at once, immediately,
in the manner of something that had been waiting under pressure for exactly this release.
100,000 lamps. That is the conservative count, the count drawn from the Westinghouse contract
and the documented lamp installation per building. Some accounts say more. The number that matters
is not the number, but the simultaneity. And the simultaneity is what the photographs cannot hold.
20,000 people made a sound that was not applause.
Applause is a decision. This was not. The involuntary sound a body produces when the
visual field is overwhelmed faster than the nervous system can process the new information.
The sound came from the chest, from the place in the chest that responds to things before the mind
has caught up. Then it became applause as the minds caught up. But for a moment, between the
lights coming on and the hands beginning to move, the crowd made the sound of pure registration.
The court of honor was white, white in a way that the word cannot quite carry. The plaster,
the composite of plaster of Paris and cement and glycerin and jute fiber,
trailed over the steel and wood frames to produce the neoclassical details,
had been finished in calcium sulfate, which is white in daylight. Under incandescent illumination
at this scale, it was not white in the way that a white wall in a room is white. It was white in
the way that the inside of a cloud is white when you are in it. Omni-directional,
sauceless, the light arriving from every surface simultaneously because every surface was generating
it. The lagoon received the light and doubled it. The water of the lagoon held the reflection
of the court of honor buildings with a precision that still water has when the air above it is still
and the light is strong enough to clarify every surface. The reflection was a second
white city, inverted, suspended below the real one. The columns and cornices were upside down
in the black water. The dome was a dome in both directions. 20,000 people were standing between
the white city and its mirror image and the light was hitting them from above and below
simultaneously. The sensation of standing in front of something that looks as if it has been there
for a hundred years. This is the part that requires attention. The buildings were temporary.
They had been built in approximately 30 months using a composite designed to last the six months
of the fair's run and then be demolished. The construction record is explicit about this.
Daniel Burnham's correspondence, the Westinghouse contract, the building permit,
all of it consistent with a temporary exhibition. The buildings were not designed to last.
They were not built to last. But under the light of 100,000 incandescent lamps,
they looked as if they had. The columns cast shadows with the sharpness of stone columns
under noon sun. The cornices had the depth of carved limestone, not the suggestion of depth,
but depth itself. The shadow falling into the recess and the cornice edge catching the light
at an angle that made the plaster surface look like something quarried. The pediments held their
weight against the sky. The way pediments hold weight when the stone behind them is the stone
they appear to be. Was it the light? The official explanation is yes. The White City's aesthetic
program depended on this. Burnham had designed it to look permanent. The official photographers
had been stationed at angles that maximized the impression of weight and permanence. The calcium
the eternal. And it performed it well enough that 20,000 people on the opening night,
and 27 million over the course of five months, went home carrying the memory of buildings
that looked like they had stood for a century. The explanation is complete. It satisfies at the
level of logic. But look at what a woman named Cecilia Wren wrote in her diary three days after
the opening. A private diary, never published, acquired in a lot of Chicago ephemera by the
same collector who would later acquire James Coburn's field note, held by the same estate
in Kenosha, Wisconsin, the same estate that dispersed in 1971. Cecilia Wren was a teacher
from Evanston, Illinois. She had attended the opening ceremony. She wrote,
I have seen paintings of Rome and of Athens, and I know what those buildings are made of.
And I know that plaster painted white cannot be the same thing. But I swear to you,
standing in that light, I could not tell the difference. It was not a painting of Rome.
It was Rome. And I know that cannot be true, and I cannot explain why my hands,
when I put them on the column near the central pavilion, felt what they felt.
She didn't describe what her hands felt. She moved on in the diary. The next paragraph
was about dinner. Cecilia Wren was 51 years old. She'd grown up in a house with limestone
foundation walls. She had spent 30 years touching chalk, slate, and the plaster ceilings of school
rooms in Evanston. Her hands knew the difference between things. She went to the central pavilion
on the third day of the fair. This is in the diary, a Tuesday afternoon. The crowds thinner
on weekday afternoons. The lake wend off the water. She walked to the nearest column
and put her palm flat against the surface. The calcium sulfate was there. She could feel it,
the slight grit, the fine crystalline texture at the very edge of fingertip sensitivity,
the specific dry quality of plaster that has been finished smooth but not polished.
That was the outer layer. That was what she expected. She had run her hands over plaster
her entire life, and she knew what plaster returned against a bare palm.
But the column was not returning what plaster returns. The first thing she noticed was the
temperature. Plaster in May, standing in the open air for three days, draws warmth from the sun
and releases it slowly but evenly. The surface should have been warm in the afternoon light.
The warmth distributed across the face of the column, the way warmth
distributes in any porous composite that absorbs solar radiation at its surface
and doesn't conduct it far. This column was warmer at the base than the face.
Warmer in the interior register, not the surface warmth of something heated from outside,
but the deeper warmth of something that generates or retains heat from within.
Stone does this. Limestone three feet thick holds its temperature differently than three
inches of plaster over wire length. The second thing was the return. When her palm pressed against
the surface, the surface pressed back. Not hard, not with any force. The specific resistance of
a thing that has mass behind it. Dense mass. Her hand against plaster over wood framing gets a vibration.
A slight give. The sensation of thickness backed by air and structural members.
Her hand against this column got stone. The pressure traveled back through her palm and
into her wrist with the quality of something continuous, something that went down through
the floor of the pavilion and kept going. She pressed harder. The column absorbed the pressure
and returned it unchanged, like pressing your palm against the side of a building
instead of a partition. She stood there for a moment, then she moved on to dinner.
She did not tell anyone what she had felt. There was no frame for it. The column was plaster over
wood. Everyone said so. The signs said so. The official program said so. Her hands said something
else and her hands were 51 years old and knew things that were hard to explain in a diary.
So she wrote the sentence and stopped and went to find her sister at the refreshment stand near
the agriculture building. The next paragraph was about dinner. The photographs are the natural
place to look and the record looked at them first. Thousands of photographs survive from
the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. Official documentation. Tourist records.
The panorama views taken by the official photographers. They are striking images.
The scale of the Court of Honor buildings reads clearly even in the compressed medium of silver
nitrate and glass. The columns are columns. The pediments are pediments. The lagoon reflection
is visible in several of the wide format shots. The buildings look permanent in all of them.
The question is whether they look more permanent than temporary construction
photographed under optimal conditions should look, or whether the photographic process itself
was doing the work. And then there are the Halstead negatives. Six glass plate negatives
donated to the Halstead photographic collection in Oak Park Illinois in 1937 by an unnamed estate.
The Halstead collection holds a private archive of Chicago ephemera.
It does not accept public inquiries and its contents are not indexed in any institutional
finding aid. The six negatives were catalogued informally. Their existence in the collection
became known through a research note in an unpublished architectural history from the early
1990s. The six glass plates show construction documentation of the manufacturers and liberal
arts building. Not finished documentation. Not the building as it appeared during the fair.
Construction documentation. Work in progress. The kind of images taken to record the building
state at a particular stage of the construction timeline. The kind of images are supervising
engineer orders when the project has reached a milestone worth recording. The manufacturers
and liberal arts building was the largest building in the world at the time of the fair.
Four hundred and forty seven meters long. More than two million square feet of interior space.
The steel and wood framing of a structure that size was a significant milestone.
The photographs should show that framing. The structural skeleton before the plaster was applied.
Or the early stages of application over completed framing. The photographs show completed facades.
Completed neoclassical facades on the manufacturers and liberal arts building.
The columns. The entablature. The decorative band course. The palasters flanking the entry
pavilion. All of it finished or nearly finished to a degree consistent with late stage construction
or completion. And the glass plates carry date codes. Not handwriting. Not a label applied later.
Open to questions of attribution. The date code is part of the manufacturing process of the glass
itself. Pressed into the edge of the plate at the point of manufacture. Indicating the period
in which the plate was produced. The six glass plates carry date codes consistent with early
1891. Physical construction at Jackson Park began in January of 1891. The official construction
timeline for the manufacturers and liberal arts building places the completion of the facade
in late 1892. Approximately two years after groundbreaking. For the facade shown in the
construction would have had to progress at a rate significantly faster than the documented timeline.
Or the photographs are showing a state of completion that the timeline cannot account for.
The official explanation exists and it is the correct place to start.
Glass plates were reused. The date code indicates plate manufacture. Not photograph exposure.
Supervising engineers sometimes staged construction photographs for official record. Documenting
completed sections in advance of the overall project schedule. These are reasonable explanations.
They account for the anomaly without requiring the timeline to be wrong. The record notes them.
The record also notes that the Halstead negatives are six plates. Not a systematic
documentation series. Six plates from what would have been a much larger documentation effort.
If the construction was being photographed at multiple stages. Six plates donated by an unnamed
estate in 1937. Six plates that resist the explanations available. In a collection that
doesn't permit the examination necessary to fully resolve the question. The photographs
were designed to make the buildings look permanent. That explanation is complete and accurate.
But now comes James Coburn. The standard account of how the white city was built
deserves its full weight before it is destabilized because it is remarkable on its own terms.
And this account is not served by treating it as a deception before the evidence requires that.
Staff plaster was an architectural achievement. The composite of plaster of Paris, cement,
glycerin and binders. Primarily jute fiber and dextrin. A starch derived adhesive.
Could be cast or troweled over wire lathe and structural framing to produce detailed decorative
surfaces with a speed that traditional stone construction couldn't match. European exposition
buildings had used similar techniques for decades. The Paris exposition universe cell of 1889
had demonstrated what temporary exhibition architecture was capable of. The Eiffel Tower
was the iron anchor of that fair. But the surrounding exhibition buildings were exercises in exactly the
kind of rapid construction grandeur that staff composite made possible. What Burnham and his
team achieved at Jackson Park in approximately 30 months was genuine. The documented construction
accounts in the inland architect from 1892 and 1893 described the pace of the work.
The crews working multiple shifts. The prefabrication of architectural details in workshops before
installation. The coordination of dozens of contractors across 690 acres of former
lakefront swamp and parkland. The compressed timeline was real. The achievement was real.
And the surfaces were what the record says they were. Staff plaster was the skin, not the skeleton.
The load bearing elements were the steel and wood frames. The plaster composite was applied
over those frames three to four inches enough to hold detailed surface treatment. Not enough to
stand on its own. A wall of plaster without its internal frame would not be a wall. It would be a
shell. And shells can be photographed to look like anything. The white city name was Burnham's
choice. The calcium sulfate surface of the staff plaster read as white in almost any
lighting condition and under the incandescent illumination of the Westinghouse Tesla system
it read as monumental as the marble of a Rome or an Athens transported to the lakefront of Chicago
in 1893. The deception was not a flaw in the project. It was the project. The white city
was designed to produce the sensation of permanence in people who knew at some level that what they
were standing in front of was temporary. The satisfaction was in the performance not the
substance. This is the explanation and it is sufficient and it is true and it accounts for
27 million people going home carrying the memory of buildings that looked like stone when they were
not stone. It accounts for everything about the white city except what James Coburn found inside
the wall. James Coburn was from Gary, Indiana. This is in the letter where he gives his address
in the heading the practical information a man includes when writing to his foreman in case a
reply is needed. He was hired by a wrecking contractor for the post fair demolition of the
1893. Coburn worked on the manufacturers and liberal arts building between December of 1893
and April of 1894. He kept field notes not a formal journal but a laborer's working record,
daily assignments, surfaces encountered, problems noted. The kind of record a careful
worker keeps in case of dispute. The field notes survive as photocopies. The originals
pass through two subsequent hands before arriving in a private collection in Kenosha, Wisconsin,
around 1950, part of a larger lot of Chicago ephemera at an estate sale. When that estate dispersed
at auction in 1971, a researcher arranged to have photocopies made of two of the three items
before dispersal. The researcher didn't publish. The originals current location hasn't been
established. The photocopies are what survive. And what survives in the photocopies across the
daily entries of a careful working man is a picture of ordinary demolition work with one
extraordinary exception. The ordinary work reads like what demolition work reads like,
arrival at the site, assignment to a section, the physical work of opening walls and removing
debris, note of what was encountered and how long it took. The language is terse. Working notes written
at the end of a long physical day have a brevity that is not literary choice. It is exhaustion
editing the unnecessary. Then, in the second week of February, 1894, had trouble today with
south section near the piers. Winter, 1894, the Manufactures and Liberal Arts building.
South Wing, the fair has been over for three months and the largest building in the world
is being unmade. James co-burns hands on the wrecking bar at seven in the morning when the
temperature on the lakefront was well below freezing and the iron of the bar was cold enough
to feel through work gloves. Not the comfortable cold of cold handled tools that have been used
for an hour and have taken some warmth from the hands. The morning cold, the cold of iron that
has been left outside overnight and has given up every calorie of retained heat to the Chicago
winter air. Through the leather and the wool lining of the gloves, the cold of the bar reached the
palms as a pressure more than a temperature. The dense, ungiving cold that reads in the hands as
weight even when the weight hasn't changed. The section of the building he was working was the
South Wing. The roof section above this area had been removed already. The demolition moved from
top down systematically. The steel trusses taken first, then the upper wall sections,
then the interior elements, leaving the exterior wall of the South Wing as the last major standing
section. Above where Coburn stood, the sky was visible, the flat gray of a Chicago winter morning.
The sky, the color of the inside of a zinc bucket, directionless light coming from all of it equally
and providing illumination without warmth. Other crews were working beyond the wall.
The sound of it reached him as percussion through the stone and plaster. Not loud, filtered by the
wall section between them, but unmistakable. The heavy thud of mauls on masonry. The specific
crack of wooden members giving way. The occasional pause that meant a man was repositioning before
the next swing. The sounds of reduction. The sounds of a building being converted from a
thing that was into a pile that could be hauled away. The smell in the opened wall was mineral.
Plaster dust has a smell that is not exactly a smell. It is more of a quality of the air.
A dryness that arrives when the calcium sulfate is broken open and the interior is exposed.
Not unpleasant. The specific dry mineral quality of a composite that has been sealed away from
moisture and now encounters the air again. And underneath that, the ghost of occupation.
The six months of the fair. The 27 million visitors. The cooking from the concessions areas
carried into the building's fabric. The chemical exhibits in the interior halls.
All of it absorbed into the pores of the wall during the fair's run.
And now slowly releasing as the wall was opened. Coburn had been doing this for weeks.
This is the thing to understand about what happened next. The body, after weeks of the
same physical operation, builds a knowledge that is not conscious and not articulate.
Not expertise. Nothing so formal as that. The body's version of expertise is simpler.
It builds a file. Every time a wrecking bar connects with the same type of construction,
the vibration that travels up the bar through the gloves into the wrists and forearms,
and up through the shoulders gets added to the file. The nervous system is a recording instrument.
And after weeks of the same surfaces, the file is complete enough that any deviation from it
is registered before the mind has finished processing the impact.
Coburn brought the bar to the section of wall. He made contact. The bar didn't respond
the way it had been responding for weeks. Not wrong in the way that an unexpected obstruction
is wrong. Not harder, exactly. Not blocked. Not the specific resistance of a structural element
encountered when the surface should have been clear. Different in a more fundamental way.
The vibration that travelled up the iron and through the gloves and into the bones of his wrists
was not the vibration he had been accumulating in his file for weeks.
The file said one thing. The wall said another. He did it again.
The same return. More complex than plaster over wire lath. The vibration was carrying
more information than the plaster should have been capable of carrying. Not just the energy
of the impact returning through the bar, but something that built after the initial contact
and sustained. The way a struck bell carries more than the energy of the striker.
The way the stone converts impact to vibration. And how much of that vibration travels back
through the tool into the hand of the person holding it. His hands were receiving something
that didn't match three weeks of demolition work on the same building. He took off the right glove.
He placed his palm flat against the surface of the wall. The plaster finish was there.
The slight grit of the calcium sulfate surface against bare skin. The crystalline texture,
just perceptible at the very edge of fingertip sensitivity. This was what he expected.
This was the outer layer of staff composite. And it felt exactly like staff composite.
But the temperature was wrong. The wall had been losing heat to the Chicago winter for months.
The building was not heated. The fair was over. The enormous stone faced rooms were open to the
winter through the sections already demolished above. A wall in those conditions should be cold at
the core. The surface should be very nearly the temperature of the air around it. The plaster
should be cold to the touch and stay cold against the bare hand. This section was not cold.
Not warm either. Not the warmth of a heated space. Something between cold and room temperature,
closer to body temperature than a wall in an unheated building in February in Chicago,
had any right to be. As if the limestone behind the plaster had been losing heat
more slowly than it should. As if there was something denser in there.
Something that had absorbed the warmth of the six months of the fair's occupation.
And hadn't yet fully surrendered it to the winter. Dense stone retains heat differently
than porous plaster. Dense limestone can hold what it has absorbed for a long time
after the source of the absorption has been removed. His palm against the wall felt the texture of
the plaster. But through the plaster, beneath it, there was a different register. Not hollow.
Not the slight give of a surface that is three or four inches of composite over wire length and
framing. Solid in a way that went deeper than the surface. The kind of solid that doesn't transmit
vibration the way surface plaster does. That absorbs the strike differently. That returns
more of the energy than it keeps. That rings rather than thuds. He stood there with his bare hand on
the wall. He stood there long enough for the temperature of the wall to settle into his palm.
For the palm to stop registering its own warmth. As the warmth of the wall.
For the distinction between his skin and the surface to clarify. He was reading the wall
the way a doctor reads something. Not examining. Not testing. But receiving. Letting it tell him.
Then he put his glove back on. Then he moved to a different section. Then,
at the end of the workday, in his field notes, he wrote, had trouble today with south section
near the pier. Harder than expected in places. Will need to note for billing. And then,
in the letter to his foreman, which came several weeks later. After the trouble had become not
an isolated incident but a pattern. It gave back more than it should have. Like ringing a pan and
hearing a bell. Some sections I could not work the standard way. In the south colonnade section,
near the base of the second pier from the east, there was stone there. Mr. H. Not staff. I do not
know how to account for it. The stone ran below the floor level. I did not dig to find where it
ended. He was not writing a mystery. He was writing documentation for a billing dispute.
He was a working man, noting a practical problem in the only language his position gave him.
The language happened to be precise. Working men whose daily occupation is the physical
differentiation of surfaces develop a precision about construction that is not literary and not
theoretical. It is functional. When James Coburn wrote the word stone, he meant stone. He had been
working with plaster for weeks. He knew the difference. The narrator does not know what
happened next. Coburn's field notes continue after this date, but they move to a different
section of the building. The south colonnade section near the second pier from the east
doesn't appear in the subsequent entries. He moved on. He didn't go back. Whether his foreman
responded to the letter is not established. There is no reply in the surviving record.
Whether the billing dispute that prompted the documentation was resolved is not established.
And then, in the final week of April, 1894, the field notes end. They end at a point where
Coburn had noted his intention to move to the northwest section of the building,
the section he hadn't yet reached. The final entry describes his assignment for the following day.
Northwest section. Ground level. There is no entry for the following day. The notebook ends.
The page after the final entry is blank. The follow-up letter he had mentioned writing.
The one that would describe what he found in the northwest section
doesn't exist in the surviving record. The collection dispersed in 1971.
The original's current location hasn't been established.
There is no record of James Coburn in any Chicago city directory after 1894.
No death certificate bearing his name has been located in the Cook County records for that period.
No labor record from any subsequent contractor project in the Chicago area has produced his name.
The record notes the absence. It doesn't fill it. What did he find in the northwest section?
March 7th, 1894. Transportation building annex. Jackson Park.
The City of Chicago Bureau of Public Works maintained forms for contractor incidents
during demolition and construction projects. The forms were standard, date, location,
nature of incident, names of injured workers, surface conditions, supervisors' notation.
They were not designed for mystery. They were designed for the insurance liability record
and the workers' compensation filings that an urban government accumulates over decades
of large-scale construction and demolition. Two workers injured on March 7th, 1894.
The incident report describes the nature of the incident. The crew was working a wall section
in the transportation building annex, grid 14. The wall section proved resistant to the
standard demolition method. The crew applied additional force.
The material gave suddenly. Two workers were struck by displaced sections.
In the field labelled material conditions contributing to incident, the superintendent
wrote in his own hand, wall section in grid 14, unexpectedly resistant,
material not consistent with expected staff construction. Crew applied additional force.
Material gave suddenly. Two workers struck by displaced sections.
Material not consistent with expected staff construction.
The superintendent who wrote this didn't know James Coburn. He hadn't read the letter to Mr. H.
He hadn't stood with his bare hand on the South Colonnade Wall and felt what Coburn felt.
He was filling out a mandatory form after two members of his crew had been hurt
and the field that asked him to describe surface conditions received an accurate answer.
He was not theorising. He was reporting. This is what two independent observers,
a demolition labourer working the manufacturers and liberal arts building
and a contractor's superintendent working the transportation building annex,
described across two months of demolition work at the Jackson Park site.
Not the same building, not the same section, not the same project and not the same vocabulary
because one was a working man writing to his foreman and the other was a supervisor
filing a mandatory form. The vocabulary was different. The observation was the same.
Material not consistent with expected staff construction. The incident report surfaced
through a footnote in an unpublished master's thesis on Chicago labour history written in 1967
at the University of Illinois Chicago. The thesis is accessible at the Richard J.
Daily Library. The source document it references isn't archived with the thesis.
It sits somewhere in the genuinely extensive, genuinely unsorted sections of the Illinois
State Archives Bureau of Public Works Holdings from the 1890 to 1910 period without a catalogue number.
The record does not know what to make of this. Two separate demolition operations,
separate buildings, separate personnel, separate months. One a laborer's private
note about a billing dispute. One a supervisor's mandatory incident report after workers were hurt.
Neither of them was investigating the White City's construction materials.
Both of them were doing their jobs and both of them noted in the process of doing their jobs
